A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COD-VAE work, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references and contains no supplement despite referring to one; v2 includes supplementary Sections A–F. The supplied documents support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original ShapeNet and Objaverse reconstruction and generation results, efficiency measurements, and encoder, decoder and pruning ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds compression comparisons, further ablations, runtime analyses, failure cases and text-conditioned generation results.

M1.justification: The original COD-VAE procedure is retained. Appendix F.4 adds a text-conditioned variant using CLIP embeddings, 128 latent vectors, two additional layers before pruning, and convolutional triplane refinement. Appendix C mainly discloses previously unspecified base-model details rather than establishing that the original architecture changed.

E1.justification: Appendix F.4 adds text-conditioned 3D generation using captioned objects, substantially extending the original reconstruction, class-conditioned generation and unconditional generation tasks. Existing ShapeNet and Objaverse coverage remains; the added per-category results concern categories already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Table 11 introduces three PerceiverIO compression configurations as evaluated comparators. Figure 11 adds qualitative comparisons against 3DTopia-XL, LN3Diff and GaussianAnything for text-conditioned generation. The original VecSet, 3DILG and GEM3D comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds protocols for near-surface IoU using 50K queries, controlled PerceiverIO comparisons, and multiresolution decoding timings at batch size 64. Text-conditioned evaluation introduces a 128-latent configuration, object filtering, approximately 20K training objects and unseen validation captions. These extend the evaluation design; newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish protocol changes.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s encoder, decoder and pruning-ratio ablations, v2 tests latent count, positional embeddings, single- versus two-stage training, and confidence- versus reconstruction-based uncertainty objectives in Table 13. It also adds near-surface pruning analysis, thin-structure failure cases, multiresolution sampling analysis and VAE runtime/resource breakdowns.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or variability across runs. The uncertainty head concerns token pruning, not statistical uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in Tables 1–7 remain unchanged, but Tables 8–14 add substantial results. For example, Table 11 reports 96.1% IoU for COD-VAE versus 94.0% for the strongest listed PerceiverIO variant, and Table 13 reports 94.4% versus 96.1% for single- and two-stage training. v2 also adds per-category scores and text-conditioned qualitative outputs.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds explicit mathematical definitions of the weighted two-stage objectives, including near-surface reconstruction weighting and normalized-feature MSE in Equations (8)–(10), beyond v1’s component-level prose description. Equations (1)–(7) remain unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims about compact latent representations, two-stage autoencoding, uncertainty-guided pruning, up to 16-fold compression and 20.8-fold generation speedup. Figure 1’s caption changes from 8-fold to 16-fold compression, but the latter claim already appeared in v1’s abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: The supplement adds interpretations of latent-size versus generation-quality tradeoffs and explanations for the training and uncertainty-objective ablations. It also discusses thin-structure failures, diminishing benefits from additional latents, VAE resource costs and possible texture extensions. Appendix F.4 explicitly limits comparisons with text-generation methods because their training data sizes and output capabilities differ.

D1.justification: Appendices C–E supply substantial missing implementation and reproducibility information: token merging, triplane reconstruction, loss weighting and clipping, normalization, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, metric thresholds and evaluation sample counts. v2 also specifies decoder patch size and replaces v1’s promised code release with a stated repository link.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references including PerceiverIO, 3DTopia-XL, GaussianAnything, DUSt3R, layer normalization and Earth Mover’s Distance. Supplementary discussion positions COD-VAE relative to generic latent compression and possible integrations with other 3D methods. The main related-work organization and central positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and narrative remain intact. Changes include sentence polishing, typo corrections, a clarified latent-decoder description, author contact information and acknowledgments. The new supplement organizes additional material into Sections A–F without extensively rewriting or reorganizing the original exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–14 and Figures 9–15, including diagnostic tables, failure cases, text-generation comparisons and expanded qualitative grids. Figures 1 and 5 are revised, with changed teaser examples, rearranged renderings and clearer Objaverse latent-count labeling. The original main-text displays largely retain their locations and structure.

improvement.justification: v1 directs readers to supplementary objectives and analyses absent from its PDF. v2 supplies essential implementation and evaluation details, tests previously unsupported design choices, adds a generic compression comparator, and documents failure and resource tradeoffs. These changes substantially improve reproducibility and support for the unchanged core results. The text-generation comparisons remain qualitative and use different training data, limiting their comparative force, but the broader documentation and diagnostic gains are substantial.
